items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "describe (command term)".
items.answer: Give a detailed account; in Paper 1 Q1, set out what the text shows without explaining it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: give a detailed account; in Paper 1 Q1, set out what the text shows without explaining it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between interpretation and observation.
items.answer: Observation records actions, words and settings as seen and heard; interpretation proposes what they mean and why they happen.
items.markingKey: Observation records actions, words and settings as seen and heard; interpretation proposes what they mean and why they happen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "In Paper 1 Q1 you should show your knowledge of other ethnographies to gain top marks." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3.
items.markingKey: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify one way in which identity matters in Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Men identify closely with their cocks, and the Balinese word for cock is used metaphorically for heroes, champions and ladies' men, so the fights express masculine identity and rivalry.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Men identify closely with their cocks, and the Balinese word for cock is used metaphorically for heroes, champions and ladies' men, so the fights express masculine identity and rivalry. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Clifford Geertz, "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" (1972; reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the corridor of the immigration office, the queue forms at 5 a.m. Men and women stand in separate lines, though no sign tells them to. A young man sells plastic folders for documents and "a place in the queue" for twenty dirhams. When the doors open at eight, a guard calls out surnames from a list nobody else can see. An older woman, Hajja Fatima, is allowed in first; people step aside for her. A Senegalese student behind me whispers: "Here you learn who matters before you even reach the desk."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an immigration office in Morocco.

Identify and describe the organisation of the queue at the immigration office. Refer closely to the text. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: The queue forms at 5 a.m.; men and women stand in separate lines without any sign; a young man sells folders and places in the queue; at eight a guard calls surnames from a hidden list; Hajja Fatima is allowed in first and people step aside for her.
items.markingKey: The queue forms at 5 a.m.; men and women stand in separate lines without any sign; a young man sells folders and places in the queue; at eight a guard calls surnames from a hidden list; Hajja Fatima is allowed in first and people step aside for her. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the corridor of the immigration office, the queue forms at 5 a.m. Men and women stand in separate lines, though no sign tells them to. A young man sells plastic folders for documents and "a place in the queue" for twenty dirhams. When the doors open at eight, a guard calls out surnames from a list nobody else can see. An older woman, Hajja Fatima, is allowed in first; people step aside for her. A Senegalese student behind me whispers: "Here you learn who matters before you even reach the desk."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an immigration office in Morocco.

Using the key concept of social relations, explain how the text shows power and hierarchy operating informally. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Unwritten rules (gender separation), an informal market in places, and the guard's private list show that access depends on informal power and knowledge rather than official procedure; respect for age and religious status (Hajja) produces precedence; the student's comment interprets the queue as a lesson in hierarchy and belonging for migrants.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Unwritten rules (gender separation), an informal market in places, and the guard's private list show that access depends on informal power and knowledge rather than official procedure; respect for age and religious status (Hajja) produces precedence; the student's comment interprets the queue as a lesson in hierarchy and belonging for migrants. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that description is less important than interpretation in Paper 1? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Interpretation earns more marks, but it depends on accurate, selective description.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: higher-mark questions (Q2, Q3) reward interpretation and comparison; concepts and analysis show understanding; interpretation must rest on accurate description; Q1 explicitly rewards description; misreading the text undermines all later answers. Suitable ethnographies include Geertz's "Deep Play", Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Interpretation earns more marks, but it depends on accurate, selective description. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Big question: "Is culture something people have, or something people do?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of culture and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Geertz's "Deep Play".
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Geertz read the cockfight as a text – "a story they tell themselves about themselves" – to be interpreted through thick description of its layered meanings. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Geertz read the cockfight as a text – "a story they tell themselves about themselves" – to be interpreted through thick description of its layered meanings. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Markbands – 9–10: perceptive, well-argued response integrating key concepts, ethnography and theory, with a reasoned conclusion; 7–8: clear argument that applies the key concept to ethnographic material and considers more than one perspective; 5–6: relevant response using a key concept and an ethnography, with some analysis; 3–4: some relevant ideas; ethnographic or conceptual support is thin or general; 1–2: limited response to the big question; assertions with little anthropological support; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why candidates should quote or refer closely to the text in Paper 1.
items.answer: Marks depend on evidence from the text; close reference shows that claims are grounded and prevents unsupported generalisation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Marks depend on evidence from the text; close reference shows that claims are grounded and prevents unsupported generalisation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Diego writes: "In Paper 1 Q1 you should show your knowledge of other ethnographies to gain top marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3.
items.markingKey: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Geertz's opening of "Deep Play" as an example, explain moving from observation to interpretation.
items.answer: Geertz begins with the police raid on a cockfight and his flight with villagers before interpreting the fight's meaning. The vivid observed episode is followed by an interpretive argument about status, showing how ethnographic texts build interpretation on description.
items.markingKey: Context (Geertz begins with the police raid on a cockfight and his flight with villagers before interpreting the fight's meaning.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the vivid observed episode is followed by an interpretive argument about status, showing how ethnographic texts build interpretation on description. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to moving from observation to interpretation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research"?
options: running comparison
discuss (command term)
observation (in an ethnographic text)
contextualisation
items.answer: contextualisation
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of contextualisation.

items.stem: Explain why candidates should choose their comparative ethnography according to the concept in the question.
items.answer: Comparison is meaningful only on a shared point; an ethnography rich in that concept allows specific, developed similarities and differences rather than vague parallels.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Comparison is meaningful only on a shared point; an ethnography rich in that concept allows specific, developed similarities and differences rather than vague parallels. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between summarising an ethnography and contextualising an ethnography.
items.answer: Contextualising states author, people, place and time briefly to situate the evidence; summarising retells the content at length, which wastes time unless linked to the comparison.
items.markingKey: Contextualising states author, people, place and time briefly to situate the evidence; summarising retells the content at length, which wastes time unless linked to the comparison. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Any ethnography can be used for any comparison question as long as it is described well." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The ethnography must be relevant to the concept in the question; a well-described but irrelevant ethnography earns few marks.
items.markingKey: The ethnography must be relevant to the concept in the question; a well-described but irrelevant ethnography earns few marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The cleaners at the hotel start before dawn. They are paid per room, not per hour, so Fatou never takes the lunch break written in her contract. She keeps her own list of "good floors" where guests leave tips and "bad floors" of business travellers. The supervisor, Mme Laurent, gives the good floors to the women who bring her pastries on Fridays. When the hotel advertised its "green policy" of not washing towels daily, Fatou laughed: "Green for them, more rooms for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a hotel in Paris.

Analyse how power shapes the cleaners' working lives. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Piece-rate pay pushes workers to forgo breaks (structural power of the employer); informal gifts (pastries) buy favour from the supervisor, so power also operates through personal relations and patronage; the green policy shows corporate rhetoric shifting costs onto workers, and Fatou's irony is a hidden critique.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Piece-rate pay pushes workers to forgo breaks (structural power of the employer); informal gifts (pastries) buy favour from the supervisor, so power also operates through personal relations and patronage; the green policy shows corporate rhetoric shifting costs onto workers, and Fatou's irony is a hidden critique. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how space, place and time is shown in Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013) and Liisa Malkki, Purity and Exile: Violence, Memory, and National Cosmology among Hutu Refugees in Tanzania (1995).
items.answer: Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border with Triqui companions and was detained by the Border Patrol, showing how the border distributes risk unequally between bodies. Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): The bounded, administered space of the camp encouraged a strong collective refugee identity, whereas dispersed town life encouraged assimilation. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far space, place and time is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border with Triqui companions and was detained by the Border Patrol, showing how the border distributes risk unequally between bodies. Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): The bounded, administered space of the camp encouraged a strong collective refugee identity, whereas dispersed town life encouraged assimilation. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far space, place and time is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "contextualisation".
items.answer: Situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: With reference to using Malkki to compare with a text about refugees, explain how it illustrates comparison through belonging and space.
items.answer: Malkki contrasts camp refugees' "mythico-history" with town refugees' fluid identities in Tanzania. It allows analysis of how the spatial setting of displacement shapes identity and belonging in both the text and the ethnography.
items.markingKey: Context (Malkki contrasts camp refugees' "mythico-history" with town refugees' fluid identities in Tanzania.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it allows analysis of how the spatial setting of displacement shapes identity and belonging in both the text and the ethnography. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparison through belonging and space.

items.stem: "Comparing a short unseen text with a whole ethnography is unfair because the two are unequal." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: The imbalance is real, but recognising it and comparing at the level of concepts turns it into an analytical strength.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: an extract offers limited evidence while a book offers depth; the text's context is unknown; the task tests the ability to identify concepts and transfer knowledge; candidates can acknowledge the limits of the extract. Suitable ethnographies include Bourgois's In Search of Respect, Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies, Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: The imbalance is real, but recognising it and comparing at the level of concepts turns it into an analytical strength. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: When observing in a public place, which is the most important ethical step?
items.answer: Avoid recording identifying details and respect people's privacy
items.markingKey: Avoid recording identifying details and respect people's privacy. Anonymity and privacy remain essential even in public.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Observing in a public place raises no ethical issues." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Even in public, people have expectations of privacy; observers must avoid identifying people, intrusive recording and harm.
items.markingKey: Even in public, people have expectations of privacy; observers must avoid identifying people, intrusive recording and harm. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why field notes should separate description from interpretation.
items.answer: Keeping them separate lets the observer check interpretations against the evidence, reconsider them later and show the reader how conclusions were reached.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Keeping them separate lets the observer check interpretations against the evidence, reconsider them later and show the reader how conclusions were reached. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Observation notes, Saturday 10.00–11.30, public library reading room. 10.04: A man in a suit chooses the table nearest the window and spreads three newspapers across it. 10.20: Two teenagers sit at the end of the same table; he moves one newspaper closer to himself without looking up. 10.41: A librarian walks past and says "Good morning, Mr Haddad." 10.55: An older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices; they put on earphones. 11.12: The man leaves; the teenagers spread out their books across the whole table within two minutes.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): observation notes written by a student in a public library.

Using evidence from the text, describe how people use the table in the reading room. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: The man spreads three newspapers across the window table; when teenagers sit, he moves one paper closer without looking up; the librarian greets him by name; an older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices and they put on earphones; after he leaves, the teenagers spread their books across the whole table within two minutes.
items.markingKey: The man spreads three newspapers across the window table; when teenagers sit, he moves one paper closer without looking up; the librarian greets him by name; an older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices and they put on earphones; after he leaves, the teenagers spread their books across the whole table within two minutes. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: With reference to Daniel Miller, A Theory of Shopping (1998) and The Comfort of Things (2008), explain how the key concept of social relations helps us to understand the use of public space.
items.answer: Routine purchases – a partner's preferred food, children's clothes – are ways of making and maintaining relationships rather than simply individual consumption.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Routine purchases – a partner's preferred food, children's clothes – are ways of making and maintaining relationships rather than simply individual consumption. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Daniel Miller, A Theory of Shopping (1998) and The Comfort of Things (2008), among households on streets in North London); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Observation notes, Saturday 10.00–11.30, public library reading room. 10.04: A man in a suit chooses the table nearest the window and spreads three newspapers across it. 10.20: Two teenagers sit at the end of the same table; he moves one newspaper closer to himself without looking up. 10.41: A librarian walks past and says "Good morning, Mr Haddad." 10.55: An older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices; they put on earphones. 11.12: The man leaves; the teenagers spread out their books across the whole table within two minutes.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): observation notes written by a student in a public library.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Consider the obligations owed to different people involved in the research.
items.answer: The student recorded a real name (Mr Haddad) heard in public, which should be removed; library users did not consent, so notes must avoid identifying details; permission from library staff is advisable; the student should reflect on their own presence. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The student recorded a real name (Mr Haddad) heard in public, which should be removed; library users did not consent, so notes must avoid identifying details; permission from library staff is advisable; the student should reflect on their own presence. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why a focused research question improves a short observation exercise.
items.answer: It tells the observer what to look for in a limited time, prevents unfocused description and allows analysis using a relevant key concept.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It tells the observer what to look for in a limited time, prevents unfocused description and allows analysis using a relevant key concept. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Augé's analysis of airports and motorways as non-places and explain what it reveals about choosing an observation site.
items.answer: Augé described how travellers pass through transit spaces guided by signs, tickets and screens. Such sites allow students to observe how space shapes interaction and identity, e.g. how people avoid or create contact in a station.
items.markingKey: Context (Augé described how travellers pass through transit spaces guided by signs, tickets and screens.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: such sites allow students to observe how space shapes interaction and identity, e.g. how people avoid or create contact in a station. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to choosing an observation site.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "competing obligations"?
options: Give a detailed account; in Paper 1 Q1, set out what the text shows without explaining it
Duties the anthropologist owes to different parties (participants, colleagues, funders, the public) that may conflict
Specific ethnographies studied, cited with author, title, people, place and time of fieldwork
Give a detailed account including reasons or causes
items.answer: Duties the anthropologist owes to different parties (participants, colleagues, funders, the public) that may conflict
items.markingKey: B. "competing obligations" is duties the anthropologist owes to different parties (participants, colleagues, funders, the public) that may conflict.

items.stem: A student claims: "A big question has one correct answer." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Big questions are open; credit goes to well-argued, ethnographically supported responses that consider alternative perspectives.
items.markingKey: Big questions are open; credit goes to well-argued, ethnographically supported responses that consider alternative perspectives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The researcher had been invited by the mining company to study "community relations" in the valley. On her first day, villagers assumed she worked for the company and refused to speak to her. She moved out of the company guesthouse and rented a room from Doña Rosa, whose son had been injured in a protest against the mine. Within weeks, protest leaders were asking her to share what she knew about the company's plans. The company manager, meanwhile, emailed asking for "a short list of key troublemakers".
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a mining region in the Andes of Peru.

Describe the different groups the researcher deals with in the text, as presented in the text. Write in your own words and keep close to the evidence in the extract.
items.answer: The mining company, which invited her to study community relations; villagers who assumed she worked for the company and refused to talk; Doña Rosa, her landlady, whose son was injured in a protest; protest leaders who asked her to share information; the company manager who asked for a list of troublemakers.
items.markingKey: The mining company, which invited her to study community relations; villagers who assumed she worked for the company and refused to talk; Doña Rosa, her landlady, whose son was injured in a protest; protest leaders who asked her to share information; the company manager who asked for a list of troublemakers. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example Bourgois's In Search of Respect, explain the relevance of power to ethical dilemmas in research.
items.answer: Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The researcher had been invited by the mining company to study "community relations" in the valley. On her first day, villagers assumed she worked for the company and refused to speak to her. She moved out of the company guesthouse and rented a room from Doña Rosa, whose son had been injured in a protest against the mine. Within weeks, protest leaders were asking her to share what she knew about the company's plans. The company manager, meanwhile, emailed asking for "a short list of key troublemakers".
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a mining region in the Andes of Peru.

Compare and contrast how power is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995)). Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: Her initial link to the company (funding, guesthouse) made villagers suspicious, so positionality limited access; moving in with Doña Rosa repositioned her within the community; both sides then try to use her as a source of information, showing how power and competing interests turn the researcher into a resource and create pressures on neutrality. Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Text: Her initial link to the company (funding, guesthouse) made villagers suspicious, so positionality limited access; moving in with Doña Rosa repositioned her within the community; both sides then try to use her as a source of information, showing how power and competing interests turn the researcher into a resource and create pressures on neutrality. Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them. Any well-contextualised ethnography is acceptable. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why ethics questions reward discussion of dilemmas rather than rules.
items.answer: Real fieldwork situations involve conflicting principles (honesty versus harm, advocacy versus neutrality) that codes cannot settle; discussing how to weigh them shows deeper understanding.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Real fieldwork situations involve conflicting principles (honesty versus harm, advocacy versus neutrality) that codes cannot settle; discussing how to weigh them shows deeper understanding. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Big questions are too broad to be answered anthropologically." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Big questions can be answered anthropologically when grounded in specific ethnographic comparison.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they invite philosophical generalisation; ethnography is specific. Arguments against: key concepts and comparison allow ethnography to speak to broad questions; anthropology has always addressed what it means to be human. Supported judgement: Big questions can be answered anthropologically when grounded in specific ethnographic comparison. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "analyse (command term)"?
options: A question about what is right in research – such as consent, harm, confidentiality or representation – raised by a particular situation
Give a detailed account; in Paper 1 Q1, set out what the text shows without explaining it
Full notes written soon after observation that describe settings, actions and words in concrete detail and separate description from interpretation
Break down in order to bring out the essential elements or structure
items.answer: Break down in order to bring out the essential elements or structure
items.markingKey: D. "analyse (command term)" is break down in order to bring out the essential elements or structure.

items.stem: In a Paper 1 comparison answer, which opening best contextualises an ethnography?
options: "Anthropologists have studied migrants."
"Holmes wrote a book about fruit."
"Holmes (2013) studied Triqui migrant farmworkers from Oaxaca on berry farms in Washington State in 2003–2005."
"In a study I read, workers were poor."
items.answer: "Holmes (2013) studied Triqui migrant farmworkers from Oaxaca on berry farms in Washington State in 2003–2005."
items.markingKey: C. Author, date, people, place and time give context.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "research question (observation)"?
options: A question about what is right in research – such as consent, harm, confidentiality or representation – raised by a particular situation
A feature shared by the text and the chosen ethnography, such as the use of hidden forms of resistance
Brief notes made during observation to record key details, words and times for later expansion
A focused question that guides what to observe, e.g. "How do customers and vendors negotiate price at the Saturday market?"
items.answer: A focused question that guides what to observe, e.g. "How do customers and vendors negotiate price at the Saturday market?"
items.markingKey: D. "research question (observation)" is a focused question that guides what to observe, e.g. "How do customers and vendors negotiate price at the Saturday market?".

items.stem: Explain the difference between an area-of-inquiry question and a big question.
items.answer: A big question addresses broad human issues across contexts (e.g. belonging); an area-of-inquiry question focuses on a defined field such as health or classification.
items.markingKey: A big question addresses broad human issues across contexts (e.g. belonging); an area-of-inquiry question focuses on a defined field such as health or classification. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between interpretation and observation.
items.answer: Observation records actions, words and settings as seen and heard; interpretation proposes what they mean and why they happen.
items.markingKey: Observation records actions, words and settings as seen and heard; interpretation proposes what they mean and why they happen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Hana writes: "Any ethnography can be used for any comparison question as long as it is described well." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The ethnography must be relevant to the concept in the question; a well-described but irrelevant ethnography earns few marks.
items.markingKey: The ethnography must be relevant to the concept in the question; a well-described but irrelevant ethnography earns few marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an overt observer and a covert observer.
items.answer: An overt observer is known to be researching; a covert observer is not. In public places observers are often not noticed, so they must take particular care with privacy and anonymity.
items.markingKey: An overt observer is known to be researching; a covert observer is not. In public places observers are often not noticed, so they must take particular care with privacy and anonymity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a big question response needs both concepts and ethnography.
items.answer: Key concepts give the analytical lens, while ethnography provides the evidence that turns a philosophical question into an anthropological argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Key concepts give the analytical lens, while ethnography provides the evidence that turns a philosophical question into an anthropological argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "An unseen text should be summarised in full before answering any question." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Answers should be selective and focused on the command term and the question; full summaries waste time and marks.
items.markingKey: Answers should be selective and focused on the command term and the question; full summaries waste time and marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Scott's Weapons of the Weak (in "Sedaka", a pseudonymous rice-growing village in Kedah, Malaysia (fieldwork 1978–1980)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: After double-cropping and combine harvesters cut work for poor villagers, they resisted through foot-dragging, gossip, pilfering and slander against rich farmers rather than open revolt.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: After double-cropping and combine harvesters cut work for poor villagers, they resisted through foot-dragging, gossip, pilfering and slander against rich farmers rather than open revolt. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (James C. Scott, Weapons of the Weak: Everyday Forms of Peasant Resistance (1985), in "Sedaka", a pseudonymous rice-growing village in Kedah, Malaysia (fieldwork 1978–1980)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Observation notes, Saturday 10.00–11.30, public library reading room. 10.04: A man in a suit chooses the table nearest the window and spreads three newspapers across it. 10.20: Two teenagers sit at the end of the same table; he moves one newspaper closer to himself without looking up. 10.41: A librarian walks past and says "Good morning, Mr Haddad." 10.55: An older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices; they put on earphones. 11.12: The man leaves; the teenagers spread out their books across the whole table within two minutes.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): observation notes written by a student in a public library.

Analyse what the notes suggest about how space is claimed in the library. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Space is claimed through objects (newspapers, books) and bodily signals rather than words; familiarity and recognition (the librarian knows Mr Haddad) give him authority over the "best" table; the teenagers negotiate by adjusting behaviour (earphones) and claim space once he leaves. Space becomes place through regular use, status and informal rules.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Space is claimed through objects (newspapers, books) and bodily signals rather than words; familiarity and recognition (the librarian knows Mr Haddad) give him authority over the "best" table; the teenagers negotiate by adjusting behaviour (earphones) and claim space once he leaves. Space becomes place through regular use, status and informal rules. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The researcher had been invited by the mining company to study "community relations" in the valley. On her first day, villagers assumed she worked for the company and refused to speak to her. She moved out of the company guesthouse and rented a room from Doña Rosa, whose son had been injured in a protest against the mine. Within weeks, protest leaders were asking her to share what she knew about the company's plans. The company manager, meanwhile, emailed asking for "a short list of key troublemakers".
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a mining region in the Andes of Peru.

Explain how the researcher's position shapes her relationships in the text, using one or more anthropological concepts. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: Her initial link to the company (funding, guesthouse) made villagers suspicious, so positionality limited access; moving in with Doña Rosa repositioned her within the community; both sides then try to use her as a source of information, showing how power and competing interests turn the researcher into a resource and create pressures on neutrality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Her initial link to the company (funding, guesthouse) made villagers suspicious, so positionality limited access; moving in with Doña Rosa repositioned her within the community; both sides then try to use her as a source of information, showing how power and competing interests turn the researcher into a resource and create pressures on neutrality. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the corridor of the immigration office, the queue forms at 5 a.m. Men and women stand in separate lines, though no sign tells them to. A young man sells plastic folders for documents and "a place in the queue" for twenty dirhams. When the doors open at eight, a guard calls out surnames from a list nobody else can see. An older woman, Hajja Fatima, is allowed in first; people step aside for her. A Senegalese student behind me whispers: "Here you learn who matters before you even reach the desk."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an immigration office in Morocco.

Explain how the text shows power and hierarchy operating informally, using one or more anthropological concepts. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Unwritten rules (gender separation), an informal market in places, and the guard's private list show that access depends on informal power and knowledge rather than official procedure; respect for age and religious status (Hajja) produces precedence; the student's comment interprets the queue as a lesson in hierarchy and belonging for migrants.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Unwritten rules (gender separation), an informal market in places, and the guard's private list show that access depends on informal power and knowledge rather than official procedure; respect for age and religious status (Hajja) produces precedence; the student's comment interprets the queue as a lesson in hierarchy and belonging for migrants. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The cleaners at the hotel start before dawn. They are paid per room, not per hour, so Fatou never takes the lunch break written in her contract. She keeps her own list of "good floors" where guests leave tips and "bad floors" of business travellers. The supervisor, Mme Laurent, gives the good floors to the women who bring her pastries on Fridays. When the hotel advertised its "green policy" of not washing towels daily, Fatou laughed: "Green for them, more rooms for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a hotel in Paris.

Describe, with examples from the text, how Fatou and the other cleaners organise their work. Refer to at least three specific details from the text.
items.answer: They start before dawn; they are paid per room, so Fatou skips the lunch break; she classifies floors as "good" (tips) and "bad" (business travellers); Mme Laurent allocates good floors to women who bring her pastries; Fatou notes the green policy means more rooms for cleaners.
items.markingKey: They start before dawn; they are paid per room, so Fatou skips the lunch break; she classifies floors as "good" (tips) and "bad" (business travellers); Mme Laurent allocates good floors to women who bring her pastries; Fatou notes the green policy means more rooms for cleaners. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Using Low's observation of plazas in San José, Costa Rica as an example, explain systematic observation of public space.
items.answer: Low mapped who used different areas of the plazas at different times and how users and officials interacted. Behavioural mapping and repeated observation showed how space was socially produced and contested, a model for small-scale observation projects.
items.markingKey: Context (Low mapped who used different areas of the plazas at different times and how users and officials interacted.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: behavioural mapping and repeated observation showed how space was socially produced and contested, a model for small-scale observation projects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to systematic observation of public space.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Simpson's "ethnographic refusal" in Mohawk Interruptus shows the ethics of representation.
items.answer: Simpson chose not to publish certain internal community matters she learned in Kahnawà:ke. She shows that responsible ethnography may involve deciding what not to write, protecting the community's sovereignty over its own knowledge.
items.markingKey: Context (Simpson chose not to publish certain internal community matters she learned in Kahnawà:ke.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: she shows that responsible ethnography may involve deciding what not to write, protecting the community's sovereignty over its own knowledge. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the ethics of representation.

With reference to social relations, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Geertz's "Deep Play". Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: Unwritten rules (gender separation), an informal market in places, and the guard's private list show that access depends on informal power and knowledge rather than official procedure; respect for age and religious status (Hajja) produces precedence; the student's comment interprets the queue as a lesson in hierarchy and belonging for migrants. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

With reference to power, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Piece-rate pay pushes workers to forgo breaks (structural power of the employer); informal gifts (pastries) buy favour from the supervisor, so power also operates through personal relations and patronage; the green policy shows corporate rhetoric shifting costs onto workers, and Fatou's irony is a hidden critique. Ethnography – Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013), with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005): Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: "How do people make places meaningful?" With reference to Augé's Non-Places and the key concept of space, place and time, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies space, place and time explicitly and uses ethnography: Augé contrasts "anthropological places", which are relational, historical and concerned with identity, with the "non-places" of supermodernity through which people pass as solitary individuals. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies space, place and time explicitly and uses ethnography: Augé contrasts "anthropological places", which are relational, historical and concerned with identity, with the "non-places" of supermodernity through which people pass as solitary individuals. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Markbands – 9–10: perceptive, well-argued response integrating key concepts, ethnography and theory, with a reasoned conclusion; 7–8: clear argument that applies the key concept to ethnographic material and considers more than one perspective; 5–6: relevant response using a key concept and an ethnography, with some analysis; 3–4: some relevant ideas; ethnographic or conceptual support is thin or general; 1–2: limited response to the big question; assertions with little anthropological support; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The researcher had been invited by the mining company to study "community relations" in the valley. On her first day, villagers assumed she worked for the company and refused to speak to her. She moved out of the company guesthouse and rented a room from Doña Rosa, whose son had been injured in a protest against the mine. Within weeks, protest leaders were asking her to share what she knew about the company's plans. The company manager, meanwhile, emailed asking for "a short list of key troublemakers".
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a mining region in the Andes of Peru.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.
items.answer: This is a classic dual-use dilemma: providing a list of "troublemakers" would breach do no harm and confidentiality and could endanger people; she must be transparent with villagers about her funding, refuse to pass on identifying information, consider whether she can continue under company funding and protect Doña Rosa's family. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: This is a classic dual-use dilemma: providing a list of "troublemakers" would breach do no harm and confidentiality and could endanger people; she must be transparent with villagers about her funding, refuse to pass on identifying information, consider whether she can continue under company funding and protect Doña Rosa's family. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: According to IB command terms, "compare and contrast" requires:
options: a description of one item only
a judgement without evidence
an account of similarities and differences between two items, referring to both throughout
a list of definitions
items.answer: an account of similarities and differences between two items, referring to both throughout
items.markingKey: C. Both items must be addressed throughout.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "contextualisation"?
options: A statement of what the ethnographer saw or heard, such as actions, words and settings
Situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research
Duties the anthropologist owes to different parties (participants, colleagues, funders, the public) that may conflict
Specific ethnographies studied, cited with author, title, people, place and time of fieldwork
items.answer: Situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research
items.markingKey: B. "contextualisation" is situating an ethnography by stating who was studied, where, when and by whom, and the wider conditions of the research.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "observation site".
items.answer: The public or semi-public location chosen for the observation exercise, such as a market, café, sports ground or place of worship
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the public or semi-public location chosen for the observation exercise, such as a market, café, sports ground or place of worship. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between an ethical dilemma and an ethical principle.
items.answer: An ethical principle is a general rule such as "do no harm"; an ethical dilemma is a specific situation in which principles conflict, requiring judgement.
items.markingKey: An ethical principle is a general rule such as "do no harm"; an ethical dilemma is a specific situation in which principles conflict, requiring judgement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "In Paper 1 Q1 you should show your knowledge of other ethnographies to gain top marks." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3.
items.markingKey: Q1 asks for description from the text; outside ethnography is not credited there and belongs in Q3. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a running comparison and an end-on comparison.
items.answer: A running comparison links the text and the ethnography point by point throughout; an end-on comparison discusses one after the other, leaving links implicit.
items.markingKey: A running comparison links the text and the ethnography point by point throughout; an end-on comparison discusses one after the other, leaving links implicit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a jotting and a full field note.
items.answer: A jotting is a brief note made during observation to aid memory; a full field note is a detailed account written soon after, describing setting, actions and words and distinguishing description from interpretation.
items.markingKey: A jotting is a brief note made during observation to aid memory; a full field note is a detailed account written soon after, describing setting, actions and words and distinguishing description from interpretation. items.stem: A student claims: "An ethics answer should list as many ethical principles as possible." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Listing without application earns little; the answer should analyse specific issues in the text and weigh obligations.

items.stem: Using Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Explain how Bourgois's In Search of Respect illustrates the concept of change. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: New York's shift from a manufacturing to a service economy left young Puerto Rican men without the jobs that had sustained their parents, unsettling masculine roles and family life.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The cleaners at the hotel start before dawn. They are paid per room, not per hour, so Fatou never takes the lunch break written in her contract. She keeps her own list of "good floors" where guests leave tips and "bad floors" of business travellers. The supervisor, Mme Laurent, gives the good floors to the women who bring her pastries on Fridays. When the hotel advertised its "green policy" of not washing towels daily, Fatou laughed: "Green for them, more rooms for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a hotel in Paris.

Using the key concept of power, explain how power shapes the cleaners' working lives. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Piece-rate pay pushes workers to forgo breaks (structural power of the employer); informal gifts (pastries) buy favour from the supervisor, so power also operates through personal relations and patronage; the green policy shows corporate rhetoric shifting costs onto workers, and Fatou's irony is a hidden critique.

Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: A student claims: "Observing in a public place raises no ethical issues." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Even in public, people have expectations of privacy; observers must avoid identifying people, intrusive recording and harm.
items.markingKey: Even in public, people have expectations of privacy; observers must avoid identifying people, intrusive recording and harm. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Holmes's border crossing with Triqui migrants shows ethical dilemmas of participation.
items.answer: Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border without documents alongside his companions and was arrested and released, while they were deported. The case raises questions about legal risk, unequal consequences for researcher and participants, and the value of shared experience for understanding.
items.markingKey: Context (Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border without documents alongside his companions and was arrested and released, while they were deported.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case raises questions about legal risk, unequal consequences for researcher and participants, and the value of shared experience for understanding. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ethical dilemmas of participation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the corridor of the immigration office, the queue forms at 5 a.m. Men and women stand in separate lines, though no sign tells them to. A young man sells plastic folders for documents and "a place in the queue" for twenty dirhams. When the doors open at eight, a guard calls out surnames from a list nobody else can see. An older woman, Hajja Fatima, is allowed in first; people step aside for her. A Senegalese student behind me whispers: "Here you learn who matters before you even reach the desk."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an immigration office in Morocco.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: People in an immigration queue may have insecure legal status; observing and writing about them requires care with consent, anonymity and avoiding exposure of the informal "place-selling" or the guard; the researcher's own status may affect how they are treated. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Hotel cleaners, often migrants with insecure contracts, risk losing work if critical comments are traced; the hotel and supervisor should be anonymised and consent obtained from the workers rather than only the management. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "A short observation exercise cannot produce valid anthropological knowledge." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: It produces limited but genuine knowledge if its limits are acknowledged.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: limited time prevents rapport and depth; the observer cannot learn insiders' meanings; focused observation reveals patterns of space and interaction; it develops ethnographic skills and reflexivity; findings can be presented as tentative. Suitable ethnographies include Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Augé's Non-Places, Low's On the Plaza. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: It produces limited but genuine knowledge if its limits are acknowledged. items.stem: "Who has the power to define a community and its boundaries?" With reference to Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus and the key concept of belonging, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies belonging explicitly and uses ethnography: Community membership rules are debated as Mohawks decide who belongs in the face of colonial definitions imposed by the Indian Act. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
